Independent directory

Find a place to get VHS, film, and photos digitized.

VHS Near Me lists local transfer shops and compares mail-in labs. The first city page covers Dallas–Fort Worth, including Flower Mound, Lewisville, and Denton. Every price is copied from the business’s own site, or the listing says to call.

What this is

People still have closets of VHS, VHS-C, Hi8, Video8, MiniDV, 8mm and Super 8 film, photo prints, slides, and negatives. The players and scanners are disappearing faster than the media. This site is a directory of places that will transfer that material to files you can actually open.

It has two halves. City pages are for drop-off and local pickup, where the tapes stay in town. The mail-in page compares companies that send a box or a label and do the work at their own lab. Use a city page when you do not want to ship the only copy. Use mail-in when you have a large, ordinary collection and you have read the current price.

How to choose

  1. Sort the formats first. A low VHS price does not mean the shop scans slides or transfers MiniDV. Read the format guides, then match the stack you actually have.
  2. Decide if the originals can travel. Local drop-off keeps a one-of-a-kind tape in the same metro area. Mail-in is a fair choice for a large box of ordinary tapes and prints. Photograph the labels and keep your own inventory before anything ships.
  3. Read the unit, not just the dollar sign. Per tape, per minute, per foot of film, and per photo are different deals. A prepaid “10 item” kit can cost more than a per-tape shop once you add the empty-box shipping, a USB drive, and discs.
  4. Ask four questions before you pay. What happens to a moldy or broken tape? Do the originals come back? Is the result an MP4 you can copy, or only a DVD? What is the turnaround this month, not the one printed on an old page?
  5. Skip copyrighted movies. Labs in this directory transfer footage and photos you own. They are not a way to copy store-bought movies or recorded television. Shops that say they will do that are a reason to walk away.

Format guides

Short practical notes on what each format is, what a finished transfer should include, and what to ask. The guides do not rank shops.

Format

VHS to digital

VHS is the large black cassette from the late 1970s through the 2000s. A useful transfer gives you a file you can copy, and it gives you the original tape back. A higher price does not recover picture detail the tape never recorded.

Read the guide

Format

Photos, slides, and negatives

Prints, slides, and negatives are three different scans. A flatbed that is fine for a 4×6 print is often a poor slide scanner. The cheap headline price is usually for loose color prints of a normal size.

Read the guide

Format

8mm film, Super 8, Hi8, and MiniDV

A metal reel of Super 8 and a small Hi8 cassette were sold in the same years and are completely different objects. Film is priced by the foot. Camcorder tapes are priced by the cassette. Mixing them up is how people get a useless quote.

Read the guide
